L4: # 28 On the Instrumental Music (ātodya)
L5: 
L6: What's in this page?
L7: 
L8: 🐎💪 32%
L9: ## Three Classes of Instruments
L10: 
L11: I shall now explain the formal aspects (lit. rule) of the instrumental music (ātodya). They are as follows:
L12: 
L13: 1. Regular musical instruments[^mg1] are of four kinds, such as ‘stringed’ (tata),[^mg2] ‘covered’ (avanaddha),[^mg3] ‘solid’ (ghana)^{【0†1】} and ‘hollow’ (suṣira).
L14: 
L15: 2. [Among these,] the ‘stringed’ are those with strings, the ‘covered’ means the drums, the ‘solid’ the cymbals and the ‘hollow’ the flutes.
L16: 3. In connexion with the dramatic performance (nāṭaka) they have threefold application: [that in which] the stringed instruments (tata) [preponderate], [that in which] the drums (avanaddha) [preponderate], and their [general] application during the dramatic performance (nāṭyakṛta).
L17: 4-5. In the Orchestra of the stringed instruments (kutapa)^{【1†2】}, [appear] the singer (gāyana) and his attendants^{【2†3】} and players of Vipañcī,^{【3†4】} Vīṇā^{【4†5】} and flute. Players of Mṛdaṅga (earthen drum), Paṇava^{【5†6】} and Dardura^{【6†7】} are [collectively] called the Orchestra of the covered instruments (lit. in the rule of the covered instruments).
L18: 6. The Orchestra related to actors and actresses (prakṛti)^{【7†8】} of the superior,’ the middling and the ordinary type, occupies different positions^{【8†9】} on the stage during the production of plays (nāṭyayoga).
L19: ## Music of all kinds embellishes the Drama
L20: 
L21: 7. Thus the song (gāna), the instrumental music (vādya) and the acting (nāṭya)^{【9†10】} having different kinds of appeals (vividhāśraya, lit. depending on different things)^{【10†11】} should be made by the producers of plays like a brilliant entity (alātacakra-pratima.).^{【11†12】}
L22: ## Characteristics of the Gāndharva
L23: 
L24: 8. That which is made by the stringed instruments and depends [as well] on various other instruments, and consists of notes (savra), Tāla (time-measure) and verbal themes (pada) should be known as the Gāndharva.^{【12†13】}
L25: 
L26: 9. As it is very much desired by gods and as it gives much pleasure to Gandharvas, it is called the Gāndharva (i.e. a thing belonging to Gandharvas.)
L27: ## Sources of the Gāndharva
L28: 
L29: 10. Its source is the human throat (lit. body), the Vīṇā and the flute (vaṃśa). I shall describe the formal aspects of (lit. arising from) their notes.
L30: 
L31: ## Three kinds of the Gāndharva
L32: 
L33: 11. The Gāndharva is of three kinds^{【13†14】}: that of the notes (svara), that of the Tāla and that of the verbal theme (pada). I shall describe the characteristics and the function of the three.
L34: ## Two Bases of Notes
L35: 
L36: 12. The notes (svara) have two bases: the human throat (lit. body) and the Vīṇā. I shall speak about the formal aspects of the notes arising from the two.
L37: ## Formal Aspects of Music of the Vīṇā
L38: 
L39: 13-14. Notes (svara)^{【14†15】}, Grāmas, Mūrchanās^{【15†16】}, Tānas^{【16†17】}, voice-registers (sthāna), Vṛttis^{【17†18】}, Overlapping (sādhāraṇa) notes. Varṇas, Alaṃkāras, Dhātus^{【18†19】}, Śrutis^{【19†20】} and Jātis which are constituted by the regular notes (vidhisvara), are available (lit. united) in the wooden Vīṇā.
L40: ## Formal Aspect of Music of the Human Throat
L41: 
L42: 15. Notes, Grāmas, Alaṃkāras, Varṇas, voice-resisters Jātis and Overlapping notes are available in the Vīṇā of the human throat.
L43: ## Aspects of the Verbal Theme in Music
L44: 
L45: 16-17. Consonants^{【20†21】}, vowels, euphonic combinations (sandhi), case-endings (vibhakti), nouns (nāma), verbs (ākhyāta), prefixes (upasarga), particles (nipāta), secondary suffixes (taddhita), and syllabic and moric metres always relate to the verbal themes of music (pada). These are of two kinds: composed (nibaddha) and improvised (anibaddha, lit. not composed).
L46: ## Twenty Aspects of the Tāla
L47: 
L48: 18-20. Now I shall speak of the Tāla^{【21†22】}. Āvāpa^{【22†23】} Niṣkrama, Vikṣepa, Praveśaka, Śamyā, Tāla, Sannipāta, Parivarta, Vastu, Mātrā, Vidārī, Aṅga, tempo (laya), Yati, Prakaraṇa, Gīti, Avayava, Mārga, Pādabhāga, and Pāṇi are the twenty^{【23†24】} formal aspects of the Tāla. These [are] in brief about the Gāndharva. Listen next in details about the same.
L49: ## The Seven Notes
L50: 
L51: On the Notes (svara):
L52: 
L53: 21. The seven notes are: Ṣaḍja (sa), Ṛṣabha (ri), Gāndhāra (ga), Madhyama (ma), Pañcama (pa), Dhaivata (dha) and Niṣāda (ni).
L54: 
L55: ## Mutual relation of the Notes
L56: 
L57: 22. [According] as they relate to an interval of [more or less] Śrutis, they are of four classes, such as Sonant^{【24†25】} (vādin), Consonant (saṃvādin)^{【25†26】} Assonant (anuvādin^{【26†27】}, and Dissonant (vivādin)^{【27†28】}.
L58: ## The Sonant and the Consonant Notes
L59: That which is an Aṃśa^{【28†29】} [note] anywhere, will in this connexion, be called there Sonant (vādin). Those two notes which are at an interval, of nine or thirteen Śrutis from each other are mutually Consonant (saṃvādin) e.g. Ṣaḍja and Madhyama, Ṣaḍja and Pañcama, Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata, Gāndhāra and Niṣada in the Ṣaḍja Grāma. Such is the case in the Madhyama Grāma, except that Ṣaḍja and Pañcama are not Consonant while Pañcama and Ṛṣabha are so. [On these there] is a [traditional] Śloka:
L60: 23. In the Madhyama Grāma, Pañcama, and Ṛṣabha are Consonant while Ṣaḍja and Pañcama are so in the Ṣaḍja Grāma [only].
L61: ## The Dissonant Notes
L62: 
L63: The notes being at an interval of [two or] twenty Śrutis are Dissonant^{【29†30】} e.g. Ṛṣabha and Gāndhāra, Dhaivata and Niṣāda.
L64: ## The Assonant Notes
L65: Now Sonant, Consonant and Dissonant notes having been determined (lit. established) the remaining ones are to be called Assonant^{【30†31】}, e.g. Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Dhaivata and Niṣāda to Ṣaḍja; Madhyama, Pañcama and Niṣāda to Ṛṣabbā; and Madhyama, Pañcama and Dhaivata to Gāndhāra; Dhaivata, Pañcama and Niṣāda to Madhyama; Dhaivata and Niṣāda to Pañcama; Ṛṣabha, Pañcama and Madhyama to Dhaivata. [All these are ] in the Ṣaḍja Grāma.
L66: In the Madhyama Grāmā too, Pañcama, Dhaivata and Niṣāda [are Assonant] to Madhyama; Ṛṣabha Ṣaḍja, and Gāndhāra to Pañcama; Ṣaḍjā, Ṛṣabha and Gāndhāra to Dhaivata; the same (Ṣāḍja, Ṛṣabha and Gāndhāra) to Niṣāda. As a note [prominently] sounds it is called Sonant; as it sounds in cosonance [with another] it is Consonant; as it sounds discordantly [to another] it is Dissonant, and as it follows [another note] it is called Assonant.
L67: These notes become low or high according to the adjustment of the strings, and the varying condition (lit. diversity) of the beam of the Vīṇā and of the sense-organs. So much about the aspects of four classes of notes.
L68: ## Description of the Two Grāmas
L69: 
L70: Now, there are two Grāmas^{【31†32】}: Ṣaḍja and Madhyama. Each of these two (lit. there) include twenty-two Śrutis in the following manner:
L71: 
L72: 24. Śrutis in the Ṣaḍja Grāma are shown as follows:—three [in Ṛṣabha],^{【32†33】} two [in Gāndhāra], four [in Madhyama], four [in Pañcama], three [in Dhaivata], two [in Niṣāda] and four [in Ṣaḍja].
L73: In the Madhyama Grāma Pañcama should be made difficient in one Śruti. The difference which occurs in Pañcama when it is raised^{【33†34】} or lowered by a Śruti and when consequential slackness^{【34†35】} or tenseness [of strings] occurs, will indicate a typical (pramāṇa) Śruti.^{【35†36】} We shall explain the system of these [Śrutis], The two Vīṇās with beams (daṇḍa) and strings of similar measure,^{【36†37】} and with similar adjustment of the latter in the Ṣaḍja Grāma should be made [ready].
L74: [Then] one of these should be tuned in the Madhyama Grāma by lowering Pañcama [by one of Śruti]. The same (Vīṇā) by adding one Śruti (lit. due to adding of one Śruti) to Pañcama will be tuned in the Ṣaḍja Grāma. This is the meaning of decreasing a Śruti (lit. thus a Śruti is decreased). Again due to the decrease of a Śruti in another [Vīṇā] Gāndhāra and Niṣāda will merge with Dhaivata and Ṛṣbha respectively, when there is an interval of two Śrutis between them.
L75: Again due to the decrease of a Śruti in another (Vīṇā) Ṛṣbha and Dhaivata will merge with Ṣaḍja and Pañcama respectively when there is an interval of [three] Śrutis. Similarly the same [one] Śruti being again decreased Pañcama, Madhyama and Ṣaḍja will merge with Madhyama, Gāndhāra and Niṣāda respectively when there is an in interval of four Śrutis between them. Thus according this system of Śrutis, [each of] the two Grāmas should be taken as consisting of twentytwo Śrutis.
L76: [The following] are the Ślokas to this effect: Śrutis in the Ṣaḍja Grāma
L77: 25-26. In the Ṣaḍja Grāma, Ṣaḍja, includes four Śrutis, Ṛṣabha three, Gāndhāra two, Madhyama four, Pañcama four, Dhaivata three and Niṣāda two.
L78: ## Śrutis in the Madhyama Grāma
L79: 
L80: 27-28. [In the Madhyama Grāma] Madhyama consists of four Śrutis. Pañcama three, Dhaivata four, Niṣāda two, Ṣaḍja four, Ṛṣabha three and Gāndhāra two Śrutis^{【37†38】}. [Thus] the system of [mutual] intervals (antara) has been explained.
L81: 
L82: ## The Mūrchanās
L83: 
L84: Now about the Mūrchanās^{【38†39】}. They are of fourteen kinds in the two Grāmas^{【39†40】}.
L85: ## Mūrchanās in the Ṣaḍja Grāma
L86: 
L87: 29-30. Based on the Ṣaḍja Grāma there are seven Mūrchanās: the first Uttaramandrā, the second Rajanī, the third Uttarāyatā, the fourth Śuddhaṣaḍjā, the fifth Matsarīkṛta, the sixth Aśvakrāntā and the seventh Abhirudgatā. The first notes of these are [respectively]: Ṣaḍja, Niṣāda, Dhaivata, Pañcama, Madhyama, Gāndhāra and Ṛṣabha in the Ṣaḍja Grāma.
L88: ## Mūrchanās in the Madhyama Grāma
L89: 
L90: In the Madhyama Grāma [occur the following Mūrchanās].
L91: 
L92: 31-32. Based on the Madhyama Grāma there are seven Mūrchanās: the first Sauvīrī the second Hariṇāśvā, the third Kalopanatā, the fourth Śuddhamadhyā, the fifth Mārgavī, the sixth Pauravī and the seventh Hṛṣyakā.
L93: 
L94: [The first] notes^{【40†41】} of these are respectively Madhyama, Gāndhāra, Ṛṣabha, Ṣaḍja, Niṣāda, Dhaivata and Pañcama.
L95: ## Initial Notes of the Mūrchanās in the two Grāmas
L96: 
L97: [Thus] the first notes of these serially are: in the Ṣaḍja Grāma—Uttaramandrā [is to begin] with Ṣaḍja, Rajanī with Niṣāda, Uttarāyatā with Dhaivata, Śuddhaṣaḍjā with Pañcama, Matsarīkṛtā with Madhyama, Aśvakrāntā with Gāndhāra, and Abhirudgatā with Ṛṣabha.
L98: And in the Madhyama Grāma—Sauvīrī [is to begin] with Madhyama, Hariṇāśvā with Gāndhāra, Kalopanatā with Ṛṣabha, Śuddhamadhyamā with Ṣaḍja, Mārgī (Mārgavī) with Niṣāda, Pauravī with Dhaivata, and Hṛṣyakā with Pañcama.
L99: ## The Four classes of Mūrchanās
L100: 
L101: Thus combined in [different] orders, the notes constitute fourteen Mūrchanās of four classes, such as heptatonic (pūrṇa, lit. full), hexatonic (ṣaḍavakṛta), pentatonic (auḍavitīkṛta) and that including the Overlapping note (sādhāraṇakṛta).
L102: 33-34. The seven notes combined in [different] orders (lit. having an order) are called [full or heptatonic] Mūrchanās. Tānas^{【41†42】} consisting of six and five notes are [respectively] called hexatone (ṣāḍava)^{【42†43】} and pentatone (auḍavita).^{【43†44】} Besides these, there is another kind of Mūrchanā which includes the Overlapping notes or is combined with the Kākalī notes or the intermediate notes (antarasvara), and this belongs to both the Grāmas (Ṣaḍja and Madhyama).
L103: The same Mūrchanā is produced (lit. accomplished) in two ways. In this connexion, Gāndhāra being reduced to Dhaivata by an increase of two Śrutis in it, [the two terms] the Grāma and the Mūrchanā become differentiated in the Ṣaḍja Grāma, and due to that, Madhyama and the notes following it, become serially reduced to Niṣāda and the notes following it. In the Madhyama Grāma too, Dhaivata being softened (curtailed in Śrutis) and Niṣāda being augmented, the two [terms] are differentiated.
L104: [In case of this Grāma too] there being an interval of the same [number of] Śrutis, the difference of terms [becomes justified]. The interval between Pañcama and Dhaivata is of four Śrutis; similarly due to an increase of Gāndhāra, the interval will be of four Śrutis. The remaining Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, Niṣāda, Ṛṣabha and Ṣaḍja become reduced [serially] to Madhyama and the notes following it. This is due to an interval of the same number of Śrutis.
L105: The system of [mutual] intervals has been explained in connexion with the system of Śrutis.
L106: ## Eighty-four Tānas of the Mūrchanās
L107: 
L108: Tānas which depend on Mūrchanās are eighty-four in number. Among these the hexatonic ones are forty-nine, and the pentatonic ones thirty-five.
L109: 
L110: ## The Hexatonic Tānas
L111: 
L112: The hexatonic ones have seven varieties, e.g. four Tānas devoid of Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Niṣāda and Pañcama in the Ṣaḍja Grāma; three Tānas devoid of Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha and Gāndhāra in the Madhyama Grāma. Thus these being worked in all, the Mūrchanās [in the two Grāmas] will give rise to forty-nine Tānas.
L113: ## The Pentatonic Tānas
L114: 
L115: The pentatonic ones have five varieties e.g. three Tānas devoid of Ṣaḍja and Pañcama, of Ṛṣabha and Pañcama, and of Gāndhāra and Niṣāda in the Ṣaḍja Grāma, two Tānas devoid of Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata, and of Gāndhāra and Niṣāda in the Madhyama Grāma. Thus these being worked in all, the pentatonic Mūrchanās [in the two Grāmas] will give rise to thirty-five Tānas, twenty-one in the Ṣaḍja Grāma and fourteen in the Madhyama Grāma.
L116: ## The Two Ways of Tānas
L117: There are two ways of working the Tāna in the string (tantrī): Entrance (praveśa) and Arrest (nigraha). The Entrance is made by sharpening (lit. emphasizing) the preceding (adhara) note and by sortening (mārdava) the succeeding (uttara) note. And the Arrest is non-touching, i.e., not touching the Madhyama note. The Mūrchanā is indicated by the Madhyama note of the Vīṇā, because it is constant (anāśī. lit. not perishable). Hence the Entrance and the Arrest [do not] relate to the Madhyama note.
L118: The variety of the Tānas and the Mūrchanās thus [arising], provides enjoyment to the hearer as well as to the musician (prayoktṛ, lit. producer). The Mūrchanā [and Tāna] are also of use [because their practice helps] the attainment of the voice-registers (sthāna-prāpti).^{【44†45】}
L119: There are three voice-registers. Their description has been given in the rules regarding the Intonation (kākū).^{【45†46】}
L120: ## The Overlapping
L121: 
L122: I shall now relate the rules regarding the Overlapping of notes (sādhāraṇa-vidhi). The Overlapping (sādhāraṇa) means the quality of a noce rising between two [consecutive] notes [in a Grāma]. Why? The thing which exists between the two [similar things, partly merging into each other] is overlapping (sādhāraṇa), e.g., the transition of a season.
L123: 35. In the shade one feels cold, but while staying in the sun one sweats (lit. the sweat comes out). [ It seems that at this time ] neither has the spring come [fully], nor has the winter gone away completely.
L124: 
L125: This is an example of the overlapping season.
L126: ## Two kinds of Overlapping
L127: 
L128: There are two kinds of Overlapping: Overlapping in notes (savarasādhāraṇa) and Overlapping in Jātis (Jātisādhāraṇa).
L129: ## The Overlapping Notes
L130: The Kākalī and the transitional note (antarasvara) are the Overlapping notes (svarasādhāraṇa). Now if two Śrutis are added to Niṣāda, it is called Kākalī Niṣāda and not Ṣaḍja; as it is a note rising between the two (pure Niṣāda and Ṣaḍja), it become Overlapping. Similarly [the two Śrutis being added to it] Gāndhāra becomes transitional Gāndhāra and not Madhyama, because it is a transitional note (antarasvara) between the two (Madhyama and Gāndhāra). Thus the Overlapping notes [occur].
L131: Why is Niṣāda called Kākalī? Because it is an indistinct second, or it is produced with [slight] pulling (akṛṣṭatva^{【46†47】}) or due to its very fineness (saukṣmya^{【47†48】}) or because it behaves like the crow’s eye (kākākṣi)^{【48†49】} and relates to the two [notes, Niṣāda and Ṣaḍja], it is called (kākalī). Just as salt among the six [kinds of] taste (rasa), is called Kṣāra (corrosive), so Niṣāda is called Kākalī, and the Overlapping note is called the transitional note.
L132: ## The Overlapping Jāti
L133: The Overlapping Jāti (jātisādhārana) [arises] from observing in another Grāma the notes which belong to the minor limbs of two or more Jātis which are in the same Grāma and have common Aṃśas. The Overlapping note (svarasàdhāraṇa) belonging to the two Grāmas (Ṣaḍja and Madhyama) is of two kinds. Why? For, occurring in the Ṣaḍja Grāma it is the Overlapping Ṣaḍja, and in the Madhyama Grāma it is Overlapping Madhyama. The Overlapping here is a special nature of the note.
L134: This is so in the Ṣaḍja Grāma, and the same [also] is the case in the Madhyama Grāma. Due to the delicacy of its production (proyoga-saukṣmya) it is fitly called Kaiśika (capillary). This is the Overlapping note which is used in Jātis where Niṣāda and Gāndhāra are weak (alpa). On these points there are the two Ślokas:
L135: 36. The transitional note (antarasvara) should always relate to the ascending scale (ārohin) and be made especially weakened (alpa), but it should never be in the descending scale (avarohin).
L136: 
L137: 37. If it is made in the descending scale whether weak or strong, the transitional notes will lead Śrutis to the Jāti-rāgas.
L138: ## The Jātis
L139: 
L140: We shall now explain the Jātis.
L141: 
L142: 38-39. The Jātis^{【49†50】} relating to the Overlapping notes are three in number: Madhyama, Pañcamī and Ṣaḍjamadhyā. Their constituent parts are Ṣaḍja, Madhyama and Pañcama of which the Pañcamī will be distinct, but weaker than the rest in its own note (i.e. Pañcama).
L143: 
L144: ## Seven Jātis in the Ṣaḍja Grāma
L145: 
L146: 40-41. The seven Jātis^{【50†51】} in the Ṣaḍja Grāma are; Ṣāḍji, Ārṣabhī, Dhaivati, Naiṣādi, Ṣaḍjodīcyavatī, Ṣaḍjakaiśikī and Ṣaḍjamadhyamā.
L147: ## Eleven Jātis in the Madhyama Grāma
L148: 
L149: 42-13. The eleven Jātis^{【51†52】} in the Madhyama Grāma are; Gāndhārī, Raktagāndhārī, Gāndhārodīcyavā, Madhyamodīcyavā, Madhyama, Pāñcamī, Gāndhārapañcamī, Āndhrī, Nandayantī, Karmāravī and Kaiśikī.
L150: 
L151: 44. There are the eighteen Jātis of which I spoke before. I shall now describe the Nyāsa (terminal note) and Apanyāsa (semi-terminal note) which they include.
L152: ## Two kinds of Jātis
L153: Of these eighteen, seven owe their names to the seven notes. They are of two kinds pure (śuddha) and modified (vikṛta). In the Ṣaḍja Grāma the pure (Jātis) are Ṣāḍjī, Ārṣabhi, Dhaivatī and Niṣādavatī (= Naiṣādī) and in the Madhyama Grāma they are Gāndhāri, Madhyama and Pañcāmī. ‘Pure’ (śuddha) in this connexion means having Svarāṃśa^{【52†53】} (= Aṃśa), Graha^{【53†54】} and Nyāsa^{【53†54】} consisting of all the [seven] notes (lit. not difficient in notes).
L154: When some of these [Jātis] lack two or more of the [prescribed] characteristics except the Nyāsa, they are called ‘modified’ (vikṛtā). Hence (lit. due to this) those indeed are pure Jātis, and these indeed are modified ones (i.e. Jātis). In the observation of the Nyāsa in the [pure], Jātis the note should be regularly Mandra; but in case the modified Jātis, there is no rule [about it]. The modified [Jātis] are eleven in number and they grow from combination.
L155: [These] eleven are formed from their mutual combination, as follows:
L156: 45. Jātis are pure as well as modified, and the [latter] arises from the combination [of other Jātis]. Among them seven are pure while the remaining eleven are modified.
L157: ## The modified Jātis
L158: 
L159: 46. I shall now speak in due order and with proper brevity, of Jātis which grow out of notes, and Aṃśas of these [pure] Jātis.
L160: 
L161: 47. The Ṣaḍja-madhyama^{【54†55】} is formed by the Ṣāḍji, the Madhyama. The Ṣaḍjakaiśiki^{【55†56】} Jāti is formed by the Ṣāḍji and the Gāndhārī.
L162: 
L163: 48. The Ṣaḍjodīcyavatī is formed by the Ṣāḍji, the Gāndhārī and the Dhaivatī combined or associated with one another.
L164:
